props.title: Three Colors: White
props.initialSlug: A penniless man plots revenge through reinvention

sections.content: Three Colors: White stands as the wickedly funny middle chapter of Krzysztof Kieślowski's Three Colors trilogy, using dark comedy to explore revenge, power, and equality. After being humiliatingly divorced in France, Polish hairdresser Karol Karol orchestrates an elaborate scheme to rebuild his life and get even with his ex-wife. Unlike the somber tone of Three Colors: Blue (1993) or the romantic complexity of Three Colors: Red (1994), White embraces absurdist humor while delivering a biting commentary on post-Communist capitalism and the economic inequality between Western and Eastern Europe.

sections.content: Zbigniew Zamachowski's brilliant performance as Karol captures both pathetic comedy and calculating determination, while Julie Delpy brings fascinating complexity to Dominique. The film's shift between Paris and Warsaw creates a stark visual contrast that mirrors Europe's economic divide. Kieślowski's trademark symbolism appears throughout - the white wedding dress, snow, and doves all reinforce themes of purity and equality while being ironically undercut by the story's darker elements. SUBHEAD: Polish New Wave Context

White connects to a broader tradition of Polish cinema dealing with post-Communist transformation. Like Man of Iron (1981) by Andrzej Wajda and Camera Buff (1979) by Kieślowski himself, it examines how political changes affect individual lives. The film's sardonic take on capitalism recalls other Eastern European dark comedies like The Death of Mr. Lazarescu (2005) and When Father Was Away on Business (1985).
